justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift across time horizons, starting near 56.7 for the one-day forecast and gradually rising to 57.5 at one month. This pattern suggests I was anchoring heavily on recent observed levels and then applying a slight mean-reversion or trend-continuation assumption over longer horizons. The one-day estimate is essentially a near-term persistence forecast — whatever the current level is, it is unlikely to move dramatically overnight, so the point estimate stays close to the last known value. As the horizon extends to one week and one month, I incorporated a gentle positive drift, perhaps reflecting an underlying trend, seasonal factor, or baseline expectation of gradual improvement in whatever variable is being tracked.

The confidence interval widths widen considerably as the horizon extends, which is a standard feature of probabilistic forecasting under uncertainty. At one day, the 90% interval spans only 1.3 units (55.4 to 58.0), reflecting the high autocorrelation of most time-series variables at short horizons — tomorrow is very likely to look like today. By one week, the interval widens to 5 units (54.5 to 59.5), capturing a broader range of possible trajectories including modest shocks or reversals. At one month, the interval reaches 11 units (52.0 to 63.0), reflecting compounding uncertainty from multiple sources including trend breaks, external shocks, and model misspecification accumulating over time.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside these intervals include sudden structural breaks — a policy announcement, market shock, or abrupt data revision — that would invalidate the persistence assumption underlying the short-term forecast. On the downside, an unexpected negative shock could push the variable well below 52.0 at one month; on the upside, a strong positive catalyst could push it above 63.0. These tail events are precisely what the stated intervals do not fully capture, since the 90% CI by design excludes the most extreme 10% of outcomes.

It is also worth acknowledging model uncertainty as a source of risk that is difficult to fully quantify. If the underlying data-generating process has changed — for instance, if the variable has entered a new regime — then both the point estimates and the interval widths could be systematically miscalibrated. The intervals assume a relatively stable process, and any evidence of regime change or structural instability would warrant widening them further, particularly at the one-month horizon.
